The second largest university library in Ljubljana is the Central Technological Library, the national library and
information hub for natural sciences and technology.
Municipal Library and other libraries
The Municipal City Library of Ljubljana, established in 2008, is the central regional library and the largest Slovenian
general public library. In 2011, it held 1,657,000 volumes, among these 1,432,000 books and a multitude of other
resources in 36 branches. Altogether, there are 5 general public libraries and over 140 specialised libraries in Ljubljana.
Besides the two largest university libraries there are libraries at individual faculties, departments and institutes of the
University of Ljubljana. The largest among them are the Central Humanist Library in the field of <color=#3366CC>humanities</color>, the Central
Social Sciences Library, the Central Economic Library in the field of <color=#3366CC>economics</color>, the Central Medical Library in the field
of <color=#3366CC>medical sciences</color>, and the Libraries of the Biotechnical Faculty in the field of <color=#3366CC>biology</color> and <color=#3366CC>biotechnology</color>.
History
The first libraries in Ljubljana were located in <color=#3366CC>monasteries</color>. The first public library was the Carniolan Estates' Library,
established in 1569 by Primož Trubar. In the 17th century, the Jesuit Library collected numerous works, particularly
about mathematics. In 1707, the Seminary Library was established; it is the first and oldest public scientific library in
Slovenia. Around 1774, after the dissolution of the Jesuits, the Lyceum Library was formed from the remains of the
Jesuit Library as well as several monastery libraries.
Science
The first society of the leading scientists and public workers in Carniola was the Dismas Fraternity (Latin: Societas
Unitorum), formed in Ljubljana in 1688. In 1693, the Academia Operosorum Labacensium was founded and lasted with
an interruption until the end of the 18th century. The next academy in Ljubljana, the Slovenian Academy of Sciences
and Arts, was not established until 1938.
Transport
Ljubljana Jože Pučnik Airport, an international airport, has flights to numerous European destinations. The destinations
are mainly European.
Ljubljana is a major hub for rail mainlines; the Pan-European Corridor V, Pan-European Corridor X and the main
European lines (E 65, E 69, E 70) intersect here. All international transit trains in Slovenia drive through the Ljubljana
hub, and all international passenger trains stop there.
The area of Ljubljana has six passenger <color=#3366CC>stations</color> and nine stops. For passengers, the Slovenian Railways company
offers the possibility to buy a daily or monthly city pass that can be used to travel between them. The Ljubljana railway
station is the central station of the hub. At the end of 2006, the Ljubljana Castle funicular started to operate.
Ljubljana lies at the intersection of Slovenia's principal motorway routes, forming the central hub of the country's
motorway network. The city is connected to the southwest by the A1 and European route E70 toward the Italian cities
of <color=#3366CC>Trieste</color> and <color=#3366CC>Venice</color>, as well as the Croatian port of Rijeka. To the north, the A1 and European route E57 link
Ljubljana with Maribor and continue toward <color=#3366CC>Graz</color> and <color=#3366CC>Vienna</color>. To the east, the A2 and European route E70 connect the
city with the Croatian capital <color=#3366CC>Zagreb</color>, from where routes extend toward <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color> and major cities of the former
Yugoslavia, including <color=#3366CC>Belgrade</color>. Finally, the A2 and European route E61 run northwest toward the Austrian cities of
<color=#3366CC>Klagenfurt</color> and <color=#3366CC>Salzburg</color>, making Ljubljana an important entry point for tourists travelling from <color=#3366CC>Northern Europe</color>.
A toll sticker system has been in use on the Ljubljana Ring Road since 1 July 2008. The centre of the city is more
difficult to access especially in the peak hours due to long arteries with traffic lights and a large number of daily
commuters. The core city centre has been closed for motor traffic since September 2007 (except for residents with
permissions), creating a <color=#3366CC>pedestrian zone</color> around Prešeren Square.
Public transport
The historical Ljubljana tram system was completed in 1901 and was replaced by buses in 1928, which were in turn
abolished and replaced by trams in 1931 with its final length of 18.5 km in 1940. In 1959, it was abolished in favor of
automobiles; the tracks were dismantled and tram cars were transferred to Osijek and Subotica. Reintroduction of an
actual tram system to Ljubljana has been proposed repeatedly in the 2000s.
Ljubljana's central bus hub is located next to the Ljubljana railway station. The city bus network, run by the Ljubljana
Passenger Transport (LPP) company, is Ljubljana's most widely used means of <color=#3366CC>public transport</color>. The number of
dedicated bus lanes is limited, which can cause problems in peak hours when traffic becomes congested.
Bus rides may be paid with the Urbana payment card (also used for the funicular) or with a mobile phone. Sometimes
the buses are called trole (referring to trolley poles), harking back to the 1951–1971 days when Ljubljana had <color=#3366CC>trolleybus</color>
(trolejbus) service. There were five trolleybus lines in Ljubljana, until 1958 alongside the tram.
Another means of public road transport in the city centre is the Cavalier (Kavalir), an electric shuttle bus vehicle
operated by LPP since May 2009. There are three such vehicles in Ljubljana. The ride is free and there are no stations
because it can stop anywhere. There is also a trackless train (tractor with wagons decorated to look like a train) for
tourists in Ljubljana, linking Cyril and Methodius Square in the city centre with Ljubljana Castle.
Cycling
There is a considerable amount of <color=#3366CC>bicycle</color> traffic in Ljubljana. Bike rental is also available. Since May 2011, the
BicikeLJ, a self-service <color=#3366CC>bicycle rental</color> system offers the residents and visitors of Ljubljana 600 bicycles and more than
600 parking spots at 60 stations in the wider city centre area. The daily number of rentals is around 2,500. There was
an option to rent a bike even before the establishment of BicikeLJ. In 2016, Ljubljana was 8th on the Copenhagenize
list.
Healthcare
Ljubljana has a rich history of discoveries in medicine and innovations in medical technology. The majority of <color=#3366CC>secondary</color>
and <color=#3366CC>tertiary care</color> in Slovenia takes place in Ljubljana. The Ljubljana University Medical Centre is the largest hospital
centre in Slovenia. The Faculty of Medicine (University of Ljubljana) and the Ljubljana Institute of Oncology are the
other two central medical institutions in Slovenia. The Ljubljana Community Health Centre is the largest health centre in
Slovenia. It has seven units at 11 locations. Since 1986, Ljubljana is part of the WHO European Healthy Cities Network.
Twin towns and sister cities
Ljubljana is <color=#3366CC>twinned</color> with:
West Bengal
West Bengal is a state in the eastern part of India. It is situated along the <color=#3366CC>Bay of Bengal</color>. In 2011, its population was
around 91 million in an area of 88752 km2, while the population estimate as of 2026 is 100.6 million. West Bengal is
the fourth-most populous and thirteenth-largest state by area in India, as well as the eighth-most populous country
subdivision of the world. As a part of the <color=#3366CC>Bengal region</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>, it borders <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color> in the east,

and <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bhutan</color> in the north. It also borders the Indian states of <color=#3366CC>Jharkhand</color>, <color=#3366CC>Odisha</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bihar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sikkim</color> and <color=#3366CC>Assam</color>.
The state capital is <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color>, the third-largest metropolis, and seventh largest city by population in India. West Bengal
includes the Darjeeling Himalayan hill region, the <color=#3366CC>Ganges delta</color>, the Rarh region, the coastal <color=#3366CC>Sundarbans</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Bay</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Bengal</color>. The state's main ethnic group are the <color=#3366CC>Bengalis</color>.
The area's early history featured a succession of Indian empires, internal conflict, and a struggle between <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> for dominance. Ancient Bengal was the site of several major Janapadas, while the earliest cities date
back to the <color=#3366CC>Vedic period</color>. The region was part of several ancient panIndian empires, including the Vangas, <color=#3366CC>Mauryans</color>,
and the <color=#3366CC>Guptas</color>. The citadel of Gauda served as the capital of the Gauda kingdom, the <color=#3366CC>Pala Empire</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Sena</color>

<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>. <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> was introduced through trade with the <color=#3366CC>Abbasid Caliphate</color>, but following the <color=#3366CC>Ghurid</color> conquests led by
Bakhtiyar Khalji and the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color>, the Muslim faith spread across the entire Bengal region.
During the <color=#3366CC>Bengal Sultanate</color>, the territory was a major trading nation in the world, and was often referred by the
Europeans as the "richest country to trade with". It was absorbed into the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> in 1576. Simultaneously,
some parts of the region were ruled by several Hindu states, and Baro-Bhuyan landlords, and part of it was briefly
overrun by the Suri Empire. Following the death of Emperor <color=#3366CC>Aurangzeb</color> in the early 1700s, the proto-industrialised
Mughal Bengal became a semi-independent state under the <color=#3366CC>Nawabs of Bengal</color>, and therefore showed signs of the first
<color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>. The region was later annexed into the Bengal Presidency by the <color=#3366CC>British East India Company</color> after
the Battle of Buxar in 1764. From 1772 to 1911, Calcutta was the capital of all of East India Company's territories and
then the capital of the entirety of <color=#3366CC>India</color> after the establishment of the Viceroyalty. From 1912 to India's Independence in
1947, it was the capital of the Bengal Province.
The region was a hotbed of the <color=#3366CC>Indian independence movement</color> and has remained one of India's great artistic and
intellectual centres. Following widespread religious violence, the Bengal Legislative Council and the Bengal Legislative
Assembly voted on the Partition of Bengal in 1947 along religious lines into two independent dominions: West Bengal,
a Hindu-majority Indian state, and East Bengal, a Muslim-majority province of <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> which later became the
independent Bangladesh. The state was also flooded with Hindu refugees from East Bengal (present-day Bangladesh)
in the decades following the 1947 <color=#3366CC>partition of India</color>, transforming its landscape and shaping its politics. The early and
prolonged exposure to British administration resulted in an expansion of <color=#3366CC>Western education</color>, culminating in
developments in science, institutional education, and social reforms in the region, including what became known as the
<color=#3366CC>Bengali Renaissance</color>. Several regional and panIndian empires throughout Bengal's history have shaped its culture,
cuisine, and architecture.
Post-Indian independence, as a <color=#3366CC>welfare state</color>, West Bengal's economy is based on <color=#3366CC>agricultural production</color> and small
and medium-sized enterprises. The state's cultural heritage, besides varied folk traditions, ranges from stalwarts in
literature including Nobel-laureate <color=#3366CC>Rabindranath Tagore</color> to scores of musicians, film-makers and artists. For several
decades, the state underwent political violence and economic stagnation after the beginning of communist rule in 1977
before it rebounded. In 2023–24, the economy of West Bengal is the sixth-largest state economy in India with a gross
state domestic product (GSDP) of, and has the country's 20th-highest GSDP per capita of as of 2020–21. Despite
being one of the fastest-growing major economies, West Bengal has struggled to attract foreign direct investment due
to adverse land acquisition policies, poor <color=#3366CC>infrastructure</color>, and red tape. It also has the 26th-highest ranking among Indian
states in <color=#3366CC>human development index</color>, with the index value being lower than the Indian average. The state government
debt of, or 37.67% of GSDP, has dropped from 40.65% since 2010–11. West Bengal has three World Heritage sites
and ranks as the eighth-most visited tourist destination in India and third-most visited state of India globally.
Etymology
The origin of the name <color=#3366CC>Bengal</color> (Bangla and Bongo in <color=#3366CC>Bengali</color>) is unknown. One theory suggests the word derives from
"Bang", the name of a <color=#3366CC>Dravidian</color> tribe that settled the region around 1000 BCE. The Bengali word Bongo might have
been derived from the ancient kingdom of Vanga (or Banga). Although some early <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit literature</color> mentions the
name Vanga, the region's early history is obscure.
In 1947, at the end of <color=#3366CC>British rule</color> over the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>, the Bengal Legislative Council and the Bengal
Legislative Assembly voted on the Partition of Bengal along religious lines into two separate entities–West Bengal,
which continued as an Indian state and East Bengal, a province of <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color>, which came to be known be as East
Pakistan and later became the independent <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color>.
In 2011, the Government of West Bengal proposed a change in the official name of the state to Paschim Banga (
Pôshchimbônggô). This is the native name of the state, literally meaning "West Bengal" in <color=#3366CC>Bengali</color>. Later on August
2016, the West Bengal Legislative Assembly passed another resolution to change the name of West Bengal to
"Bengal" in <color=#3366CC>English</color> and "Bangla" in Bengali. Despite the Trinamool Congress government's efforts to forge a
consensus on the name change resolution, the <color=#3366CC>Indian National Congress</color>, the Left Front and the <color=#3366CC>Bharatiya Janata Party</color>
opposed the resolution. However, the central government has turned down the proposal maintaining the state should
have one single name for all languages instead of three and it should not be the same as that of any other territory
(pointing out that the name 'Bangla' may create confusion with neighbouring <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color>).
History
Ancient and classical period
<color=#3366CC>Stone Age</color> tools dating back 20,000 years have been excavated in the state, showing human occupation 8,000 years
earlier than scholars had thought. According to the Indian epic <color=#3366CC>Mahabharata</color>, the region was part of the Vanga
kingdom. Several <color=#3366CC>Vedic</color> realms were present in the Bengal region, including Vanga, Rarh, Pundravardhana and the
Suhma kingdom. One of the earliest foreign references to Bengal is a mention by the <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greeks</color> around 100 BCE
of a land named Gangaridai located at the mouths of the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color>. Bengal had overseas trade relations with
Suvarnabhumi (Burma, Lower <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color>, the Lower <color=#3366CC>Malay Peninsula</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sumatra</color>). According to the Sri Lankan
chronicle Mahavamsa, Prince Vijaya (c. 543 – c. 505 BCE), a Vanga kingdom prince, conquered Lanka (modern-day
Sri Lanka) and named the country Sinhala kingdom.
The kingdom of <color=#3366CC>Magadha</color> was formed in the 7th century BCE, consisting of the regions now comprising <color=#3366CC>Bihar</color> and
Bengal. It was one of the four main kingdoms of India at the time during the lives of <color=#3366CC>Mahavira</color>, the principal figure of

<color=#3366CC>Jainism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gautama Buddha</color>, founder of <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>. It consisted of several janapadas, or kingdoms. Under <color=#3366CC>Ashoka</color>,
the <color=#3366CC>Maurya Empire</color> of Magadha in the 3rd century BCE extended over nearly all of <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>, including <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>
and parts of <color=#3366CC>Balochistan</color>. From the 3rd to the 6th centuries CE, the kingdom of Magadha served as the seat of the
<color=#3366CC>Gupta Empire</color>.
Two kingdoms—Vanga or Samatata, and Gauda—are said in some texts to have appeared after the end of the Gupta
Empire although details of their ascendancy are uncertain. The first recorded independent king of Bengal was
<color=#3366CC>Shashanka</color>, who reigned in the early 7th century. Shashanka is often recorded in Buddhist annals as an intolerant
Hindu ruler noted for his persecution of the Buddhists. He murdered Rajyavardhana, the Buddhist king of Thanesar,
and is noted for destroying the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, and replacing Buddha statues with <color=#3366CC>Shiva</color> <color=#3366CC>lingams</color>. After a
period of anarchy, the <color=#3366CC>Pala dynasty</color> ruled the region for four-hundred years which began in the 8th century. A shorter
reign of the Hindu <color=#3366CC>Sena dynasty</color> followed.
<color=#3366CC>Rajendra Chola I</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Chola dynasty</color> invaded some areas of Bengal between 1021 and 1023.
<color=#3366CC>Islam</color> was introduced through trade with the <color=#3366CC>Abbasid Caliphate</color>. Following the <color=#3366CC>Ghurid</color> conquests led by Muhammad bin
Bakhtiyar Khalji and the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color>, it spread across the entire Bengal region. <color=#3366CC>Mosques</color>,
<color=#3366CC>madrasas</color> and khanqahs were built throughout these stages. During the Islamic <color=#3366CC>Bengal Sultanate</color>, founded in 1352,
Bengal was a major trading nation in the world and was often referred by the Europeans as the richest country to trade
with. Later, in 1576, it was absorbed into the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color>.
Medieval and early modern periods
Subsequent Muslim conquests further helped Islam to spread throughout the region. It was ruled by dynasties of the
Bengal Sultanate and feudal lords under the Delhi Sultanate for the next few hundred years. The Bengal Sultanate was
interrupted for twenty years by a Hindu uprising under Raja Ganesha. In the 16th century, Mughal general Islam Khan
conquered Bengal. Administration by governors appointed by the court of the Mughal Empire gave way to
semi-independence under the Nawabs of Murshidabad, who nominally respected the sovereignty of the Mughals in
<color=#3366CC>Delhi</color>. Several independent Hindu states were established in Bengal during the Mughal period, including those of
Pratapaditya of Jessore District and Raja Sitaram Ray of <color=#3366CC>Bardhaman</color>. Following the death of Emperor <color=#3366CC>Aurangzeb</color> and
the Governor of Bengal, Shaista Khan, the proto-industrialised Mughal Bengal became a semi-independent state under
the <color=#3366CC>Nawabs of Bengal</color>, and showed signs of the world's first <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>. The Koch dynasty in northern Bengal
flourished during the 16th and 17th centuries; it weathered the Mughals and survived until the advent of the British
colonial era.
Colonial period
Several European traders reached this area in the late 15th century. The <color=#3366CC>British East India Company</color> defeated Siraj
ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab, in the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Plassey</color> in 1757. The company gained the right to collect
revenue in Bengal subah (province) in 1765 with the signing of the treaty between the East India company and the
Mughal emperor following the Battle of Buxar in 1764. The Bengal Presidency was established in 1765; it later
incorporated all British-controlled territory north of the Central Provinces (now <color=#3366CC>Madhya Pradesh</color>), from the mouths of

the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Brahmaputra</color> to the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Punjab</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Bengal famine of 1770</color> claimed millions of
lives due to tax policies enacted by the British company. <color=#3366CC>Calcutta</color>, the headquarters of the East India company, was
named the capital of British-held territories in India in 1773. The failed <color=#3366CC>Indian rebellion of 1857</color> originated nearby
Calcutta, and resulted in a transfer of authority to the British Crown, which was administered by the Viceroy of India.
The <color=#3366CC>Bengal Renaissance</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Brahmo Samaj</color> socio-cultural reform movements significantly influenced the cultural
and economic life of Bengal. Between 1905 and 1911 an abortive attempt was made to partition the province of Bengal
into two zones. Years later, Bengal then suffered from the <color=#3366CC>Great Bengal famine</color> in 1943, which claimed three million
lives during World War II. Bengalis played a major role in the <color=#3366CC>Indian independence movement</color>, in which revolutionary
groups such as Anushilan Samiti and Jugantar were dominant. Armed attempts against the <color=#3366CC>British Raj</color> from Bengal
reached a climax when news of <color=#3366CC>Subhas Chandra Bose</color> leading the Indian National Army (INA) against the British
reached Bengal. The Indian National Army was subsequently routed by the British.
Indian independence and afterwards
When India <color=#3366CC>gained independence</color> in 1947, Bengal was partitioned along religious lines. The western part went to the
Dominion of India and was named West Bengal. The eastern part went to the Dominion of Pakistan as a province
called East Bengal (later renamed to East Pakistan in 1956), that became the independent nation of <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color> in
1971. In 1950, the Princely State of Cooch Behar was merged with West Bengal. Later in 1955, the former <color=#3366CC>French</color>
<color=#3366CC>enclave</color> of Chandannagar, which had passed into Indian control after 1950, was integrated into West Bengal. Few
portions of Bihar were also subsequently merged with West Bengal. Both West and East Bengal experienced large
influxes of refugees during and after the <color=#3366CC>partition</color> in 1947. Refugee resettlement and related issues continued to play a
significant role in the politics and socio-economic condition of the state.
During the 1970s and 1980s, severe power shortages, strikes and a violent <color=#3366CC>Marxist</color>–<color=#3366CC>Maoist</color> movement by groups
known as the Naxalites damaged much of the infrastructure, leading to a period of economic stagnation and
<color=#3366CC>deindustrialisation</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh Liberation War</color> of 1971 resulted in an influx of millions of refugees to West Bengal,
causing a further significant strain on its infrastructure. The 1974 smallpox epidemic killed thousands. West Bengal
politics underwent a major change when the Left Front (LF) won the 1977 assembly election, defeating the incumbent
<color=#3366CC>Indian National Congress</color>. The Left Front, led by the Communist Party of India (Marxist), governed the state next for
more than three decades.
The state's economic recovery gathered momentum after the <color=#3366CC>central government</color> introduced economic liberalisations in
the mid-1990s. This was aided by the advent of information technology and IT-enabled services. Beginning in the
mid-2000s, armed insurgents conducted minor terrorist attacks in some parts of the state. Clashes with the
administration took place at several controversial locations over the issue of industrial land acquisition. This became a
decisive reason behind the defeat of the ruling Left Front government in the 2011 assembly election. Although the
economy was severely damaged during the years of unrest in the LF rule, the state has steadily managed to revive its
economy. It has shown improvement regarding bandhs (strikes) and educational infrastructure. Significant strides have
been made in reducing unemployment, though the state suffers from substandard healthcare services, a lack of
socio-economic development, poor infrastructure, unemployment (persistent) and civil violence. In 2006, the state's
healthcare system was severely criticised in the aftermath of the West Bengal blood test kit scam.
Geography
West Bengal is on the eastern bottleneck of India, stretching from the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color> in the north to the <color=#3366CC>Bay of Bengal</color> in the
south. The state has a total area of 88752 km2. The Darjeeling Himalayan hill region in the northern extreme of the
state is a part of the eastern Himalayas mountain range. In this region is Sandakphu, which, at 3636 m, is the highest
peak of the state. The narrow Terai region separates the hills from the North Bengal plains, which in turn transitions into
the <color=#3366CC>Ganges delta</color> towards the south. The Rarh region intervenes between the Ganges delta in the east and the western
plateau and high lands. A small coastal region is in the extreme south, while the <color=#3366CC>Sundarbans</color> <color=#3366CC>mangrove</color> forests form a
geographical landmark at the <color=#3366CC>Ganges delta</color>.
The main river in West Bengal is the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color>, which divides into two branches. One branch enters Bangladesh as the
<color=#3366CC>Padma</color>, or Pôdda, while the other flows through West Bengal as the Bhagirathi River and Hooghly River. The Farakka
barrage over the Ganges feeds the Hooghly branch of the river by a feeder canal. Its water flow management has been
a source of lingering dispute between India and Bangladesh. The <color=#3366CC>Teesta</color>, Torsa, Jaldhaka and Mahananda rivers are in
the northern hilly region. The western plateau region has rivers like the Damodar, Ajay and Kangsabati. The Ganges
delta and the Sundarbans area have numerous rivers and creeks. Pollution of the Ganges from waste dumped
indiscriminately into the river is a major problem. Damodar, a tributary of the Ganges and once known as the "Sorrow of
Bengal" (due to its frequent floods), has several dams under the Damodar Valley Project. At least nine districts in the
state suffer from arsenic contamination of groundwater, and as of 2017, an estimated 1.04 crore people were affected
by arsenic poisoning.
West Bengal's climate varies from <color=#3366CC>tropical savanna</color> in the southern portions to <color=#3366CC>humid subtropical</color> in the north. The main
weather seasons are <color=#3366CC>summer</color>, the rainy season, a short <color=#3366CC>autumn</color> and <color=#3366CC>winter</color>. While the summer in the delta region is
noted for excessive humidity, the western highlands experience a dry summer like <color=#3366CC>northern India</color>. The highest daytime
temperatures range from 38 to 45 °C. At night, a cool southerly breeze carries moisture from the Bay of Bengal. In early
summer, brief squalls and thunderstorms known as Kalbaisakhi, or Nor'westers, often occur. West Bengal receives the
Bay of Bengal branch of the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean monsoon</color> that moves in a southeast to northwest direction. Monsoons bring
rain to the whole state from June to September. Heavy rainfall of above 250 cm is observed in the Darjeeling,
Jalpaiguri, and Cooch Behar district. During the arrival of the monsoons, low pressure in the Bay of Bengal region often
leads to the formation of storms in the coastal areas. Winter (December–January) is mild over the plains with average
minimum temperatures of 15 °C. A cold and dry northern wind blows in the winter, substantially lowering the humidity
level. The Darjeeling Himalayan hill region experiences a harsh winter, with occasional snowfall.
Flora and fauna
The "India State of Forest Report 2017", recorded forest area in the state as 16847 sqkm, while in 2013, forest area
was 16805 sqkm, which was 18.93% of the state's geographical area, compared to the then national average of
21.23%. Reserves, protected and unclassed forests constitute 59.4%, 31.8% and 8.9%, respectively, of forested areas,
as of 2009. Part of the world's largest <color=#3366CC>mangrove forest</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Sundarbans</color> in southern West Bengal.
From a phytogeographic viewpoint, the southern part of West Bengal can be divided into two regions: the <color=#3366CC>Gangetic</color>
<color=#3366CC>plain</color> and the <color=#3366CC>littoral</color> mangrove forests of the Sundarbans. The <color=#3366CC>alluvial soil</color> of the Gangetic plain, combined with
favourable rainfall, makes this region especially fertile. Much of the vegetation of the western part of the state has
similar species composition with the plants of the Chota Nagpur plateau in the adjoining state of <color=#3366CC>Jharkhand</color>. The
predominant commercial tree species is Shorea robusta, commonly known as the sal tree. The coastal region of Purba
Medinipur exhibits coastal vegetation where the predominant tree is the Casuarina. A notable tree from the Sundarbans
is the ubiquitous sundari (Heritiera fomes), from which the forest gets its name.
The distribution of vegetation in northern West Bengal is dictated by elevation and <color=#3366CC>precipitation</color>. For example, the
foothills of the Himalayas, the Dooars, are densely wooded with sal and other tropical evergreen trees. Above an
elevation of 1000 m, the forest becomes predominantly subtropical. In Darjeeling, which is above 1500 m, <color=#3366CC>temperate</color>
<color=#3366CC>forest</color> trees like <color=#3366CC>oaks</color>, <color=#3366CC>conifers</color> and <color=#3366CC>rhododendrons</color> predominate.
3.26% of the geographical area of West Bengal is protected land, comprising fifteen wildlife sanctuaries and five
national parks—<color=#3366CC>Sundarbans National Park</color>, Buxa Tiger Reserve, Gorumara National Park, Neora Valley National Park

and Singalila National Park. Extant wildlife includes <color=#3366CC>Indian rhinoceros</color>, Indian elephant, <color=#3366CC>deer</color>, <color=#3366CC>leopard</color>, <color=#3366CC>gaur</color>, <color=#3366CC>tiger</color> and
<color=#3366CC>crocodiles</color>, as well as many bird species. <color=#3366CC>Migratory birds</color> come to the state during the winter. The high-altitude forests

of Singalila National Park shelter <color=#3366CC>barking deer</color>, <color=#3366CC>red panda</color>, chinkara, <color=#3366CC>takin</color>, <color=#3366CC>serow</color>, <color=#3366CC>pangolin</color>, minivet and kalij pheasants.
The Sundarbans are noted for a reserve project devoted to conserving the endangered <color=#3366CC>Bengal tiger</color>, although the
forest hosts many other endangered species such as the Gangetic dolphin, river terrapin and <color=#3366CC>estuarine crocodile</color>. The
mangrove forest also acts as a natural fish nursery, supporting <color=#3366CC>coastal fishes</color> along the Bay of Bengal. Recognising its
special conservation value, the Sundarbans area has been declared a Biosphere Reserve.
Demographics
According to the provisional results of the 2011 national census, West Bengal is the fourth-most-populous state in India
with a population of 91,347,736 (7.55% of India's population). The state's 2001–2011 decennial population growth rate
was 13.93%, lower than the 1991–2001 growth rate of 17.8% and lower than the national rate of 17.64%. The gender
ratio is 947 females per 1,000 males. As of 2011, West Bengal had a <color=#3366CC>population density</color> of 1029 PD/km2 making it the
second-most densely populated state in India, after <color=#3366CC>Bihar</color>.
The literacy rate is 77.08%, higher than the national rate of 74.04%. Data from 2010 to 2014 showed the <color=#3366CC>life</color>
<color=#3366CC>expectancy</color> in the state was 70.2 years, higher than the national value of 67.9. The proportion of people living below
poverty line in 2013 was 19.98%, a decline from 31.8% a decade prior. Scheduled castes and tribes form 28.6% and
5.8% of the population, respectively, in rural areas and 19.9% and 1.5%, respectively, in urban areas.
In September 2017, West Bengal achieved 100% electrification, after some remote villages in the Sunderbans became
the last to be electrified.
As of September 2017, of 125 towns and cities in Bengal, 76 have achieved open defecation free (ODF) status. All
towns in the districts of: Nadia, North 24 Parganas, Hooghly, Bardhaman and East Medinipur are ODF zones, with
Nadia becoming the first ODF district in the state in April 2015.
A 2013 study conducted in three districts of West Bengal found that accessing private health services to treat illness
had a disastrous impact on households. This indicates the importance of the public provision of health services to
mitigate poverty and the impact of illness on poor households.
The latest Sample Registration System (SRS) statistical report shows that West Bengal has the lowest fertility rate
among Indian states. West Bengal's total fertility rate (TFR) was 1.6, lower than neighbouring Bihar's 3.4, which is the
highest in the entire country. Bengal's TFR of 1.6 roughly equals that of <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Bengalis</color>, consisting of Bengali Hindus, Bengali Muslims, Bengali Christians and a few Bengali Buddhists, comprise the
majority of the population. Marwari, Maithili and Bhojpuri speakers are scattered throughout the state; various
indigenous ethnic Buddhist communities such as the Sherpas, Bhutias, Lepchas, Tamangs, Yolmos and ethnic
<color=#3366CC>Tibetans</color> can be found in the Darjeeling Himalayan hill region. Native Khortha speakers are found in Malda district.
Surjapuri, a language considered to be a mix of Maithili and Bengali, is spoken across northern parts of the state. The
Darjeeling Hills are mainly inhabited by various <color=#3366CC>Gorkha</color> communities who overwhelmingly speak <color=#3366CC>Nepali</color> (also known as
Gorkhali), although there are some who retain their ancestral languages like Lepcha. West Bengal is also home to
indigenous tribal <color=#3366CC>Adivasis</color> such as: Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Bhumij, Lodha, Kol and Toto.
There are a small number of ethnic minorities primarily in the state capital, including but not limited to <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tamils</color>,
Maharashtrians, Odias, Malayalis, Gujaratis, Anglo-Indians, Armenians, <color=#3366CC>Jews</color>, <color=#3366CC>Punjabis</color> and <color=#3366CC>Parsis</color>. India's sole
<color=#3366CC>Chinatown</color> is in eastern Kolkata.
Languages
The state's official languages are <color=#3366CC>Bengali</color> and <color=#3366CC>English</color> meanwhile <color=#3366CC>Nepali</color> has an additional official status in the three
subdivisions of Darjeeling district. In 2012, the state government passed a bill granting additional official status to <color=#3366CC>Hindi</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Odia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Punjabi</color>, Santali and <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color> in areas where speakers exceed 10% of the population. In 2019, another bill was
passed by the government to include Kamtapuri, Kurmali and Rajbanshi as additional official languages in blocks,
divisions or districts where the speakers exceed 10% of the population. On 24 December 2020, Chief Minister Mamata
Banerjee announced <color=#3366CC>Telugu</color> as an additional official language. As of the 2011 census, 86.22% of the population spoke
<color=#3366CC>Bengali</color>, 5.00% <color=#3366CC>Hindi</color>, 2.66% Santali, 1.82% <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color> and 1.26% <color=#3366CC>Nepali</color> as their first language.
Religion
West Bengal is religiously diverse, with regional cultural and religious specificities. Although Hindus are the
predominant community, the state has a large minority Muslim population. Christians, Buddhists and others form a
minuscule part of the population. As of 2011, <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color> is the most common religion, with adherents representing
70.54% of the total state population. <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, the second-most common religion, has 27.01% adherents of the total state
population. Three of West Bengal's districts: Murshidabad, Malda and Uttar Dinajpur, are Muslim-majority. <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> and other religions make up the remainder. Buddhism remains a widely followed religion in the
<color=#3366CC>Himalayan region</color> of the Darjeeling hills; almost the entirety of West Bengal's Buddhist population is from this region.
Christianity is mainly found among the tea garden tribes at tea plantations scattered throughout the Dooars of
Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri and Alipurduar districts.
The Hindu population of West Bengal is 64,385,546 while the Muslim population is 24,654,825, according to the 2011
census.
Government and politics
West Bengal is governed through a <color=#3366CC>parliamentary system</color> of <color=#3366CC>representative democracy</color>, a feature the state shares with
other Indian states. <color=#3366CC>Universal suffrage</color> is granted to its residents. There are three branches in the state's government
namely <color=#3366CC>legislature</color>, <color=#3366CC>executive</color> and judiciary. The West Bengal Legislative Assembly, consists of elected members and
special office bearers such as the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, who are elected by the members. Assembly meetings
are presided over by the Speaker, or the Deputy Speaker in the Speaker's absence. The state's judiciary is composed
of the Calcutta High Court and a system of lower courts. <color=#3366CC>Executive authority</color> is vested in the Council of Ministers
headed by the Chief Minister although the titular head of government is the Governor.
The Governor is the <color=#3366CC>Head of State</color> appointed by the President of India. The leader of the party or coalition with a
majority in the Legislative Assembly is appointed as the Chief Minister by the Governor. The Council of Ministers is
appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister. The Council of Ministers reports to the Legislative
Assembly. The Assembly is unicameral with 295 members, or MLAs, including one nominated from the Anglo-Indian
community. Terms of office run for five years unless the Assembly is dissolved before the completion of the term.
Auxiliary authorities known as panchayats, for which local body elections are regularly held, govern local affairs. The
state contributes 42 seats to the Lok Sabha and 16 seats to the Rajya Sabha of the <color=#3366CC>Indian Parliament</color>.
Politics in West Bengal is contested by political parties such as the Trinamool Congress (TMC), Bharatiya Janata Party
(BJP), <color=#3366CC>Indian National Congress</color> (INC), and the Left Front alliance (led by the Communist Party of India (Marxist) or
CPI(M)). Following the election in 2011, the Trinamool Congress and Indian National Congress coalition under Mamata
Banerjee of the Trinamool Congress was elected to power with 225 seats in the legislature.
Prior to this, West Bengal was ruled by the Left Front for 34 years (1977–2011), making it the world's longest-running
democratically elected <color=#3366CC>communist</color> government. Banerjee was re-elected twice as Chief Minister in the 2016 election
and 2021 election with 211 and 215 seats respectively, an absolute majority by the Trinamool Congress. In the 2026
election, the Bharatiya Janata Party formed the government for the first time, winning 207 seats, with Suvendu Adhikari
becoming the Chief Minister. The state has one autonomous region, the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration.
Districts and cities
Districts
As of 2023 11 1 West Bengal is divided into 23 districts.
Each district is governed by a district collector or district magistrate, appointed by either the Indian Administrative
Service (IAS) or the West Bengal Civil Service (WBCS). Each district is subdivided into sub-divisions, governed by a
Sub-Divisional Magistrate, and again into blocks. Blocks consists of panchayats (village councils) and town
municipalities.
Cities
The capital and largest city of the state is <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color>—the third-largest <color=#3366CC>urban agglomeration</color> and the seventh-largest city in
India. <color=#3366CC>Asansol</color> is the second-largest city and urban agglomeration in West Bengal.
Major planned cities of West Bengal include Bidhannagar, New Town, Kalyani, Haldia, <color=#3366CC>Durgapur</color> and Kharagpur.
Kolkata has some planned neighbourhoods like New Garia, Tollygunge, and Lake Town. <color=#3366CC>Siliguri</color> is an economically
important city, strategically located in the northeastern Siliguri Corridor (Chicken's Neck) of India. Other cities of
significance in West Bengal include Barrackpore, <color=#3366CC>Baharampur</color>, Basirhat, <color=#3366CC>Bardhaman</color>, <color=#3366CC>Howrah</color>, Chandannagar,
<color=#3366CC>Jalpaiguri</color>, Haldia and Purulia etc.
Economy
As of 2015, West Bengal has the sixth-highest Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) in India. GSDP at current prices
(base 2004–2005) has increased from Rs 2,086.56 billion in 2004–05 to Rs 8,00,868 crores in 2014–2015, reaching Rs
10,21,000 crores in 2017–18. GSDP per cent growth at current prices varied from a 10.3% low in 2010–2011 to a
17.11% high in 2013–2014. The growth rate was 13.35% in 2014–2015. The state's per capita income has lagged the
all India average for over two decades. As of 2014–2015, per capita Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) at current
prices was Rs 78,903. Per-capita NSDP growth rate at current prices varied from a 9.4% low in 2010–2011 to a
16.15% high in 2013–2014. The growth rate was 12.62% in 2014–2015.
In 2015–2016, the percentage share of Gross Value Added (GVA) of factor cost to measure economic activity at the
constant price (base year 2011–2012) for each sector was as follows—Agriculture-Forestry and Fishery–14.84%,
Industry–18.51% and Services–66.65%. A observation was drawn that there has been a slow but steady decline in the
percentage share of industry and agriculture over the years. Agriculture is the leading economic sector in West Bengal.

<color=#3366CC>Rice</color> is the state's principal food crop. Its other top crops are <color=#3366CC>potato</color>, <color=#3366CC>jute</color>, <color=#3366CC>sugarcane</color> and <color=#3366CC>wheat</color>. <color=#3366CC>Tea</color> is produced
commercially in northern districts; the region is well known for Darjeeling and other high-quality teas.
State industries are localised in the Kolkata region, the mineral-rich western highlands, and the Haldia Port region. The
Durgapur-Asansol colliery belt is home to a number of steel plants. Important <color=#3366CC>manufacturing industries</color>
include–engineering products, electronics, electrical equipment, cables, steel, leather, textiles, jewellery, <color=#3366CC>frigates</color>,
automobiles, railway coaches and <color=#3366CC>wagons</color>. The Durgapur centre has established several industries in the areas of tea,
sugar, <color=#3366CC>chemicals</color> and <color=#3366CC>fertilisers</color>. Natural resources like tea and jute in nearby areas have made West Bengal a major
centre for the jute and tea industries.
Years after independence, West Bengal is dependent on the <color=#3366CC>central government</color> for assistance to meet its demands for
food; food production remained stagnant, and the Indian green revolution bypassed the state. However, there has been
a significant increase in food production since the 1980s and the state now has a surplus of grains. The state's share of
total industrial output in India was 9.8% in 1980–1981, declining to 5% by 1997–1998. In contrast, the service sector
has grown at a rate higher than the national rate. The state's total financial debt stood at as of 2011.
In the period 2004–2010, the average GSDP growth rate was 13.9% (calculated in <color=#3366CC>Indian rupee</color> terms) lower than
15.5%, the average for all states of the country.
The economy of West Bengal has witnessed many surprising changes in direction. The agricultural sector in particular
rose to 8.33% in 2010–11 before tumbling to 4.01% in 2012–13. Many major industries such as the Uttarpara
Hindustan Motors car manufacturing unit, the jute industry, and the Haldia Petrochemicals unit experienced shutdowns
in 2014. In the same year, plans for a 300 billion Jindal Steel project was mothballed. The state's tea industry has also
witnessed shutdowns for financial and political reasons. Also its tourism industry was negatively impacted in 2017
because of the Gorkhaland agitation.
However, over the years due to effective changes in the stance towards industrialisation, ease of doing business has
improved in West Bengal. Steps are being taken to remedy this situation by promoting West Bengal as an investment
destination. A leather complex has been built in Kolkata. Smart cities are being planned close to Kolkata, and major
roadway projects are in the offing to revive the economy. West Bengal was only able to attract 2% of the Foreign direct
investment (FDI) in the 2000s.
In 2024–2025, West Bengal's NSDP grew by 9.86% to Rs 16,32,000 crores with an improvement over the 8.94%
growth recorded in previous fiscal year (FY). In the annual <color=#3366CC>state budget</color> allocation for this FY, West Bengal's
government allocated Rs 22,620 crores to Agriculture and Allied activities of which Rs 5,800 crores was allocated for
farmers' financial support and Rs 1,200 crores was allocated for crop insurance; Rs 47,470 crores was allocated for
Education, Sports, Arts, and Culture of which Rs 18,029 crores was allocated to aid private <color=#3366CC>secondary schools</color> and Rs
7,732 crores was allocated to aid private <color=#3366CC>primary schools</color>. The state's industrial sector grew by 7.3% which exceeded
that FY's national average of 6.2%.
In March 2025, Haldia Petrochemicals was exploring to open a <color=#3366CC>polycarbonate</color> production plant by investing Rs 8,500
crores. In July that year, the state government announced that it attracted Rs 1,33,000 crores from private investors
and created 1,08,000 jobs across iron and steel, energy (oil and gas), and <color=#3366CC>logistics</color> sectors. The state also organized its
eighth global summit which the large industries received an investment of Rs 23,94,595 crores.
As of 2025–2026, West Bengal is India's sixth-largest economy with a projected GSDP of Rs 20,30,000 crores. The
current GVA is as follows—Agriculture–55%, Industry–24%, and Services–55%.
For the FY 2026–27, the GSDP was projected to be Rs 21,48,224 crores with an year-on-year growth of 8% meanwhile
the state debt was projected to be reaching Rs 8,15,000 crores.
Culture
Literature
The <color=#3366CC>Bengali language</color> boasts a rich literary heritage it shares with neighbouring <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color>. West Bengal has a long
tradition of folk literature, evidenced by the Charyapada, a collection of <color=#3366CC>Buddhist mystic</color> songs dating back to the 10th
and 11th centuries; Mangalkavya, a collection of Hindu narrative poetry composed around the 13th century;
Shreekrishna Kirtana, a pastoral <color=#3366CC>Vaishnava</color> drama in verse composed by Boru Chandidas; Thakurmar Jhuli, a
collection of Bengali folk and fairy tales compiled by Dakshinaranjan Mitra Majumder; and stories of Gopal Bhar, a court
<color=#3366CC>jester</color> in medieval Bengal.
In the 19th and 20th centuries, <color=#3366CC>Bengali literature</color> was modernised in the works of authors such as <color=#3366CC>Bankim Chandra</color>
<color=#3366CC>Chattopadhyay</color>, whose works marked a departure from the traditional verse-oriented writings prevalent in that period;
Michael Madhusudan Dutt, a pioneer in Bengali drama who introduced the use of blank verse; and <color=#3366CC>Rabindranath</color>
<color=#3366CC>Tagore</color>, who reshaped <color=#3366CC>Bengali literature</color> and music. <color=#3366CC>Indian art</color> saw the introduction of Contextual Modernism in the late
19th and early 20th centuries. Other notable figures include <color=#3366CC>Kazi Nazrul Islam</color>, whose compositions form the
avant-garde genre of Nazrul Sangeet, Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, whose works on contemporary social practices in
Bengal are widely acclaimed, and Manik Bandyopadhyay, who is considered one of the leading lights of modern
Bengali fiction.
In modern times, Jibanananda Das has been acknowledged as "the premier poet of the post-Tagore era in India".
Other writers include–<color=#3366CC>Bibhutibhushan Bandopadhyay</color>, best known for his work <color=#3366CC>Pather Panchali</color>, which was later
adapted into a Bengali film of the same name by <color=#3366CC>Satyajit Ray</color>; Tarashankar Bandopadhyay, well known for his portrayal
of the lower strata of society; and Ashapurna Devi, Shirshendu Mukhopadhyay, Saradindu Bandopadhyay, Buddhadeb
Guha, Mahashweta Devi, Samaresh Majumdar, Sanjeev Chattopadhyay, Shakti Chattopadhyay, Buddhadeb Basu, Joy
Goswami and Sunil Gangopadhyay.
Music and dance
A notable music tradition is the Baul music, practised by the Bauls, a sect of mystic minstrels. Other folk music forms
include Gombhira and Bhawaiya. Folk music in West Bengal is often accompanied by the ektara, a one-stringed
instrument. Shyama Sangeet is a genre of devotional songs, praising the Hindu goddess <color=#3366CC>Kali</color>; <color=#3366CC>Kirtan</color> refers to the
devotional group songs performed in dedication to the Hindu god <color=#3366CC>Krishna</color>. Rabindra Sangeet, songs composed and
written by Rabindranath Tagore, and Nazrul Geeti (by Kazi Nazrul Islam) are popular. Also just as other states in
<color=#3366CC>northern India</color>, West Bengal has a heritage in <color=#3366CC>Hindustani classical music</color>.
Other significant songwriters and their music include–Dwijendralal Ray with his most notable song being "Dhana
Dhanya Pushpa Bhara", Atul Prasad Sen, Rajanikanta Sen, and adhunik or modern music from films and other
composers. From the early 1990s, new genres of music have emerged, including what has been called Bengali
Jeebonmukhi Gaan (a modern genre based on <color=#3366CC>realism</color>). Bengali dance forms draw from folk traditions, especially with
those of the <color=#3366CC>tribal groups</color>, as well as the broader <color=#3366CC>Indian dance traditions</color>. Chhau dance of Purulia is an uncommon form
of masked dance.
Films
West Bengali films are shot mostly in studios in the Kolkata neighbourhood of Tollygunge; the name "Tollywood"
(similar to <color=#3366CC>Hollywood</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bollywood</color>) is derived from that name. The Bengali film industry is well known for its <color=#3366CC>art films</color>,
and has produced acclaimed directors like <color=#3366CC>Satyajit Ray</color>, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest filmmakers of
the 20th century; <color=#3366CC>Mrinal Sen</color>, whose films were known for their artistic depiction of social reality; Tapan Sinha, and
<color=#3366CC>Ritwik Ghatak</color>.
Some contemporary directors include veterans such as Buddhadeb Dasgupta, Tarun Majumdar, Goutam Ghose,
Aparna Sen, Rituparno Ghosh, and a newer pool of directors such as Kaushik Ganguly and Srijit Mukherji.
Uttam Kumar was the most popular lead actor in both Tollywood as well as Bollywood for decades, and his romantic
pairing with actress Suchitra Sen in films attained legendary status. <color=#3366CC>Soumitra Chatterjee</color>, who acted in many Satyajit
Ray-films, and Prosenjit Chatterjee are among other popular lead male actors. As of 2020, Bengali films have won
India's annual National Film Award for Best Feature Film twenty-two times in sixty seven years, the highest among all
Indian languages.
Fine arts
There are significant examples of <color=#3366CC>fine arts</color> in Bengal from earlier times, including the terracotta art of Hindu temples
and the Kalighat paintings. Bengal has been the vanguard of <color=#3366CC>modernism</color> in fine arts. <color=#3366CC>Abanindranath Tagore</color>, called the
father of modern Indian art, started the Bengal School of Art, which had one of its goals as to promote the development
of styles of art outside the European realist tradition that had been taught in <color=#3366CC>art colleges</color> under the <color=#3366CC>British colonial</color>
<color=#3366CC>administration</color>. This movement had many adherents which include but not limited to– Gaganendranath Tagore,
<color=#3366CC>Ramkinkar Baij</color>, Jamini Roy and Rabindranath Tagore. After Indian Independence, important groups such as the
Calcutta Group and the Society of Contemporary Artists were formed in West Bengal, and it later had a significant
impact on the <color=#3366CC>art scene</color> in India.
Reformist heritage
The capital, Kolkata, was the workplace of several social reformers, including <color=#3366CC>Raja Ram Mohan Roy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iswar Chandra</color>
<color=#3366CC>Vidyasagar</color> and <color=#3366CC>Swami Vivekananda</color>. Their social reforms eventually led to a cultural atmosphere that made it possible
for practices like sati, <color=#3366CC>dowry</color>, and <color=#3366CC>caste-based discrimination</color>, or untouchability, to be abolished. The region was also
home to several religious teachers, such as <color=#3366CC>Chaitanya</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ramakrishna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Prabhupada</color> and <color=#3366CC>Paramahansa Yogananda</color>.
Cuisine
<color=#3366CC>Rice</color> and <color=#3366CC>fish</color> are traditional favourite foods, leading to a popular saying in <color=#3366CC>Bengali</color>, "machhe bhate bangali", which
translates to "fish and rice make a Bengali". Bengal's vast repertoire of fish-based dishes includes <color=#3366CC>hilsa</color> preparations, a
favourite among Bengalis; pabda, <color=#3366CC>chingdi</color>, lotte, rui (rohu), katla, bata, and shutki (<color=#3366CC>dried fish</color>). There are numerous
ways of cooking a fish depending upon its texture, size, fat content and bones. Most of the people also consume <color=#3366CC>eggs</color>,

<color=#3366CC>chicken</color>, <color=#3366CC>mutton</color>, and <color=#3366CC>shrimp</color>. Panta bhat (rice soaked overnight in water) with <color=#3366CC>onions</color> and <color=#3366CC>green chillies</color> is a traditional
dish consumed in rural areas.

Common spices found in a Bengali kitchen include posto, <color=#3366CC>cumin</color>, ajmoda (radhuni), <color=#3366CC>bay leaf</color>, mustard, <color=#3366CC>ginger</color>, <color=#3366CC>garlic</color>,
<color=#3366CC>green chillies</color> and <color=#3366CC>turmeric</color>. Sweets occupy an important place in the diet of Bengalis and at their social ceremonies.
Bengalis make distinctive <color=#3366CC>sweetmeats</color> from milk products, including Rôshogolla, Chômchôm, Kalojam and several
kinds of sondesh. Pitha, a kind of sweet cake, bread, or <color=#3366CC>dim sum</color>, are specialties of the winter season. Sweets such as
narkel-naru (<color=#3366CC>coconut</color> laddu), til-naru (<color=#3366CC>sesame</color> laddu), moa (particularly Jaynagarer Moa) and payesh are prepared
during Bengali festivals such as Lakshmi puja. Popular <color=#3366CC>street foods</color> include Aloor Chop, Beguni, Kati roll, Kolkata
biryani, and phuchka.
Clothing
Bengali women commonly wear the <color=#3366CC>sari</color>, often distinctly designed according to local cultural customs. In urban areas,
many women and men wear western attire. Among men, western dress has a greater acceptance. Particularly on
cultural occasions such as festivals and events, men also wear traditional costumes such as the panjabi with dhuti
while women wear salwar kameez or sari.
West Bengal produces several varieties of <color=#3366CC>cotton</color> and <color=#3366CC>silk</color> saris in the country. <color=#3366CC>Handlooms</color> are a popular way for the
state's rural population to earn a living through <color=#3366CC>weaving</color>. Every district has weaving clusters, which are home to <color=#3366CC>artisan</color>
communities, each specialising in specific varieties of handloom weaving. Notable handloom saris include Tant,
Jamdani, Garad, Korial, Baluchari, Tussar, Shantipuri and Murshidabad silk.
Festivals
Durga Puja is the largest, most popular and widely celebrated festival in West Bengal. The five-day-long colourful
Hindu festival features fiery celebrations across the state. Pandals are erected in various <color=#3366CC>cities</color>, <color=#3366CC>towns</color>, and <color=#3366CC>villages</color>
throughout West Bengal. The city of Kolkata transforms at the time of Durga Puja. It is decked up in <color=#3366CC>lighting</color> decorations
and thousands of colourful pandals are set up where effigies of the goddess <color=#3366CC>Durga</color> and her four children namely

goddess <color=#3366CC>Lakshmi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saraswati</color>, god <color=#3366CC>Ganesha</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Kartikeya</color> are displayed and worshipped. The idols of all the 5 deities
are brought in from Kumortuli, where idol-makers work throughout the year to fashion its clay models. Since
independence in 1947, Durga Puja has slowly changed into more of a glamorous carnival-like festival than a religious
one. Today people of diverse religious and ethnic backgrounds partake in the festivities. On Vijayadashami, the last
day of the festival, the effigies are paraded through the streets with riotous pageantry before being immersed into the
rivers.
Rath Yatra is a Hindu festival which celebrates Jagannath, a form of <color=#3366CC>Krishna</color>. It is celebrated with much fanfare in
Kolkata as well as in rural Bengal. Images of Jagannath are set upon a chariot and pulled through the streets.
Other major festivals of West Bengal include–<color=#3366CC>Poila Baishakh</color>, the Bengali new year; <color=#3366CC>Dolyatra</color> or <color=#3366CC>Holi</color>, the festival of
lights; Poush Parbon, Kali Puja, Nabadwip Shakta Rash (Raas Yatra), Saraswati Puja, <color=#3366CC>Deepavali</color>, Lakshmi Puja,
Janmashtami, Jagaddhatri Puja, Vishwakarma Puja, Bhai Phonta, Rakhi Bandhan, Kalpataru Day, Shivratri, Ganesh
Chathurthi, Maghotsav, Karam festival, Kartik Puja, Akshay Tritiya, Guru Purnima, <color=#3366CC>Annapurna</color> Puja, Charak Puja,

Gajan, <color=#3366CC>Buddha Purnima</color>, <color=#3366CC>Christmas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eid ul-Fitr</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eid ul-Adha</color> and Muharram. Some other important cultural events (or
holidays) include Rabindra Jayanti, Kolkata Book Fair, Kolkata Film Festival, and Nazrul Jayanti.
<color=#3366CC>Eid al-Fitr</color> is the most important Muslim festival in West Bengal. They celebrate the end of <color=#3366CC>Ramadan</color> with prayers,
alms-giving, shopping, gift-giving, and feasting.
Christmas, called Bôŗodin (Great day) is perhaps the next major festival celebrated in Kolkata, after Durga Puja.
Although Hinduism is the major religion in the state, people show significant passion to the festival. Just like Durga
Puja, Christmas in Kolkata is an occasion when all communities and people of every religion take part. Large masses
of people go to parks, gardens, museums, parties, <color=#3366CC>fairs</color>, churches and other places to celebrate the day. A lot of Hindus
go to Hindu temples and the festival is celebrated there too with specific rituals. The state tourism department
organises a gala Christmas Festival every year in Park Street. The whole of Park Street is hung with colourful lights,
and food stalls sell cakes, chocolates, <color=#3366CC>Chinese cuisine</color> (Indo-chinese food), <color=#3366CC>momo</color>, and various other items. The state

invites musical groups from <color=#3366CC>Darjeeling</color> and other <color=#3366CC>North East India</color> states to perform <color=#3366CC>choir</color> <color=#3366CC>recitals</color>, carols, and <color=#3366CC>jazz</color>
numbers.
<color=#3366CC>Buddha Purnima</color>, which marks the birth of <color=#3366CC>Gautama Buddha</color>, is one of the most important Hindu/Buddhist festivals and
is celebrated with much gusto in the Darjeeling hills. On this day, processions begin at the various <color=#3366CC>Buddhist</color>
<color=#3366CC>monasteries</color>, or gumpas, and congregate at the Chowrasta (Darjeeling) Mall. The Lamas chant mantras and sound
their <color=#3366CC>bugles</color> meanwhile students as well as people from every community carry the holy books or pustaks on their
heads. Besides Buddha Purnima, Dashain, or Dusshera, Holi, Diwali, Losar, Namsoong or the Lepcha New Year, and
Losoong are the other major festivals of the Darjeeling Himalayan region.
Each year between July and August or Shravana (month) at Tarakeswar Yatra, nearly 3 million devotees come from
various parts of India, bringing holy water of Ganga with them in order to offer it to the Hindu god, <color=#3366CC>Shiva</color>.
Poush Mela is a popular winter festival of Shantiniketan, with performances of folk music, Baul songs, dance, and
theatre taking place throughout the town.
Gangasagar Mela coincides with the Makar Sankranti, and hundreds of thousands of Hindu pilgrims congregate where
the river Ganges meets the sea to bathe during this fervent festival.
Transport
As of 2011, the total length of surface roads in West Bengal was over 92023 km; national highways comprise 2578 km
and state highways 2393 km. In 2006, the road density of the state was 103.69 km/km2, higher than the national
average of 74.7 km/km2.
As of 2011, the total railway route length was around 4481 km. <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color> is the headquarters of three zones of the <color=#3366CC>Indian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Railways</color>—Eastern Railway and South Eastern Railway and the <color=#3366CC>Kolkata Metro</color>, which is the newly formed 17th zone of
the Indian Railways. The Northeast Frontier Railway (NFR) serves the northern parts of the state. The Kolkata metro is
the country's first <color=#3366CC>underground railway</color>. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, part of NFR, is a UNESCO <color=#3366CC>World Heritage</color>
<color=#3366CC>Site</color>.
Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport at Dum Dum, Kolkata, is the state's largest airport. Bagdogra Airport
near <color=#3366CC>Siliguri</color> is a customs airport that offers international service to <color=#3366CC>Bhutan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color>, besides regular domestic
service. Kazi Nazrul Islam Airport, India's first private sector airport, serves the twin cities of <color=#3366CC>Asansol</color>-<color=#3366CC>Durgapur</color> at
Andal, Paschim Bardhaman.
Kolkata is a major river port in eastern India. The Kolkata Port Trust manages the Kolkata and the Haldia docks. There
is passenger service to Port Blair on the <color=#3366CC>Andaman and Nicobar Islands</color>. <color=#3366CC>Cargo ship</color> service operates to other ports in
India and abroad, operated by the Shipping Corporation of India (SCI). <color=#3366CC>Ferries</color> are a principal mode of transport in the
southern part of the state, especially in the Sundarbans area. Kolkata is the only city in India to have trams as a mode
of transport; these are operated by the Calcutta Tramways Company.
Several government-owned organisations operate bus services in the state, including: the Calcutta State Transport
Corporation, the North Bengal State Transport Corporation, the South Bengal State Transport Corporation, the West
Bengal Surface Transport Corporation and the Calcutta Tramways Company. There are also private bus companies.
The railway system is a nationalised service without any private investment. Hired forms of transport include metered
taxis and <color=#3366CC>auto rickshaws</color>, which often ply specific routes in cities. In most of the state, cycle rickshaws and in Kolkata,
hand-pulled rickshaws and electric rickshaws are used for short-distance travel.
Education
West Bengal schools are run by the state government or by <color=#3366CC>private organisations</color>, including religious institutions.
Instruction is mainly in English or <color=#3366CC>Bengali</color>, though <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color> is also used, especially in Central Kolkata. <color=#3366CC>Secondary schools</color>
are affiliated with the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations (CISCE), the Central Board for Secondary
Education (CBSE), the National Institute of Open School (NIOS), West Bengal Board of Secondary Education, or the
West Bengal Board of Madrasah Education.
As of 2016, 85% of children within the 6-17 years age group attend school (86% do so in <color=#3366CC>urban areas</color> and 84% in <color=#3366CC>rural</color>
<color=#3366CC>areas</color>). School attendance is almost universal among the 6–14 years age group, which drops to 70% within the 15–17
years age group. There is a <color=#3366CC>gender disparity</color> in school attendance in the 6–14 years age group, by which more girls
than boys are attending school. In West Bengal, 71% of women aged 15–49 years and 81% of men aged 15–49 years
are literate. Only 14% of women aged 15–49 years in the state have completed 12 or more years of schooling,
compared with 22% of men. 22% of women and 14% of men aged 15–49 years have never attended school.
Some of the notable schools in Kolkata are–Ramakrishna Mission Narendrapur, Baranagore Ramakrishna Mission,
Sister Nivedita Girls' School, Hindu School, Hare School, La Martiniere Calcutta, Calcutta Boys' School, St. James'
School (Kolkata), South Point School, St. Xavier's Collegiate School, Loreto House, and Loreto Convent. In a 2014
review by the Education World magazine, some of these schools are ranked among the best schools in the country.
Many of the schools in Kolkata and <color=#3366CC>Darjeeling</color> are colonial-era establishments housed in buildings that are exemplars
of <color=#3366CC>neo-classical architecture</color>. Darjeeling's schools include: St. Paul's, St. Joseph's North Point, Goethals Memorial
School, and Dow Hill in Kurseong.
West Bengal has eighteen universities. Kolkata has played a pioneering role in the development of the modern
<color=#3366CC>education system in India</color>. It was the gateway to the revolution of European education during the <color=#3366CC>British Raj</color>. <color=#3366CC>William</color>
<color=#3366CC>Jones</color> established the Asiatic Society in 1794 to promote oriental studies. Various reformers and educationalists such
as <color=#3366CC>Ram Mohan Roy</color>, David Hare, <color=#3366CC>Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar</color>, Alexander Duff and William Carey played leading roles
in setting up modern schools and colleges in the city.
The <color=#3366CC>University of Calcutta</color>, the oldest and one of the most prestigious public universities in India, has 136 affiliated
colleges. Fort William College was established in 1810. The Hindu College (now Presidency University) was
established in 1817. The Lady Brabourne College was established in 1939. The Scottish Church College, the oldest
Christian <color=#3366CC>liberal arts</color> college in <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>, started in 1830. The Vidyasagar College was established in 1872 and was
the first purely Indian-run private college in <color=#3366CC>India</color>. In 1855, the Hindu College was renamed to the Presidency College.
The state government granted it university status in 2010 and it was renamed as Presidency University. Kazi Nazrul
University was established in 2012. The University of Calcutta and Jadavpur University are prestigious technical
universities. Visva-Bharati University at Santiniketan is a central university and an institution of national importance.
Other higher education institutes of importance in West Bengal include–St. Xavier's College, Indian Institute of Foreign
Trade (IIFT), Indian Institute of Management Calcutta (the first IIM), Indian Institute of Science Education and
Research, Kolkata (IISER), Indian Statistical Institute (ISI), Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (the first <color=#3366CC>IIT</color>),
Indian Institute of Engineering Science and Technology, Shibpur (the first IIEST), Indian Institute of Information
Technology, Kalyani (IIIT), Medical College, Kolkata, National Institute of Technology, Durgapur (NIT), National Institute
of Technical Teachers' Training and Research, Kolkata (NITTTR), National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and
Research, Kolkata (NIPER), and West Bengal National University of Juridical Sciences (NUJS). In 2003, the state
government supported the creation of West Bengal University of Technology (MAKAUT), West Bengal University of
Health Sciences (WBUHS), West Bengal State University (WBSU), and Gour Banga University (UGB).
Jadavpur University (JU) (Focus area—Mobile Computing and Communication, and <color=#3366CC>Nano-science</color>), and the University
of Calcutta (Modern Biology) are among two of the fifteen universities selected under the "University with Potential for
Excellence" scheme. University of Calcutta (Focus Area—Electro-Physiological and Neuro-imaging studies including
<color=#3366CC>mathematical modelling</color>) has also been selected under the "Centre with Potential for Excellence in a Particular Area"
scheme.
In addition, the state is home to Kalyani University, The University of Burdwan, Vidyasagar University, and North
Bengal University all well established and nationally renowned schools that cover education needs at the district level.
Apart from this there is a Deemed university run by the Ramakrishna Mission named Ramakrishna Mission
Vivekananda University (RKMVERI) at Belur Math.
Also there are several research institutes in Kolkata. The Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS) is the
first research institute in <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>. <color=#3366CC>C. V. Raman</color> was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1930 for his discovery (Raman Effect)
done at the IACS. The Bose Institute, Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP), S. N. Bose National Centre for Basic
Sciences (SNBNCBS), Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (IICB), Central Glass and Ceramic Research Institute
(CGCRI), Central Mechanical Engineering Research Institute (CMERI) Durgapur, Central Research Institute for Jute
and Allied Fibers (CRIJAF), National Institute of Research on Jute and Allied Fibre Technology (NIRJAFT), Central
Inland Fisheries Research Institute (CIFRI), National Institute of Biomedical Genomics (NIBMG) Kalyani, and the
Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC) are the other significant institutions of the state.
Notable scholars who were born, worked, or studied in the geographic area of the state include <color=#3366CC>physicists</color> such as
<color=#3366CC>Satyendra Nath Bose</color>, <color=#3366CC>Meghnad Saha</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Jagadish Chandra Bose</color>; chemist Prafulla Chandra Roy; statisticians
Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis and Anil Kumar Gain; physician Upendranath Brahmachari; educator Ashutosh
Mukherjee; and Nobel laureates <color=#3366CC>Rabindranath Tagore</color>, C. V. Raman, <color=#3366CC>Amartya Sen</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Abhijit Banerjee</color>
Media
In 2005, West Bengal had a total of 505 published newspapers, of which 389 were in Bengali. Ananda Bazar Patrika, a
daily published in <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color> with 1,277,801 daily copies, has the largest circulation for a single-edition, regional language
newspaper in India. Other major Bengali newspapers are: Bartaman, Ei Samay, Sangbad Pratidin, Aajkaal and
Uttarbanga Sambad. Major English language newspapers include The Telegraph, <color=#3366CC>The Times of India</color>, Hindustan
Times, <color=#3366CC>The Hindu</color>, The Statesman, The Indian Express and Asian Age. Some important financial dailies such as <color=#3366CC>The</color>
<color=#3366CC>Economic Times</color>, Financial Express, Business Line and Business Standard are widely circulated. Vernacular
newspapers such as those in Hindi, Nepali, <color=#3366CC>Gujarati</color>, Odia, Urdu and Punjabi also exist.
DD Bangla is the state-owned television broadcaster. Multi system operators provide a mix of Bengali, Nepali, Hindi,
English and international channels via <color=#3366CC>cable</color>. Bengali 24-hour television news channels include ABP Ananda, News18
Bangla, Republic Bangla, Kolkata TV, News Time, Zee 24 Ghanta, TV9 Bangla, Calcutta News and Channel 10. All
India Radio is a public radio station. Private <color=#3366CC>FM</color> stations are available only in cities like Kolkata, <color=#3366CC>Siliguri</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Asansol</color>.
Vodafone Idea, Airtel, BSNL, Jio are all of the available <color=#3366CC>cellular</color> phone providers. Broadband Internet is available in
select towns and cities, and is provided by the state-run BSNL and by other private companies. Dial-up access is also
provided throughout the state by BSNL and other providers.
Sports
Netaji Indoor Stadium was completed in January 1975 and was constructed specifically to host the 1975 World Table
Tennis Championships, which were held at the venue that year. The stadium has also hosted other major events,
including the state funeral service of <color=#3366CC>Mother Teresa</color> on 13 September 1997.
<color=#3366CC>Cricket</color> and <color=#3366CC>association football</color> are popular. West Bengal, unlike most other states of India, is noted for its passion and
patronage of football. <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color> is one of the major centres for football in India and houses top national clubs such as
Mohun Bagan Super Giant, East Bengal Club and Mohammedan Sporting Club.
West Bengal has several large stadiums. Eden Gardens was one of only two 100,000-seat cricket stadiums in the
world; renovations before the 2011 Cricket World Cup reduced the capacity to 66,000. The stadium is the home to
various cricket teams such as the Kolkata Knight Riders, the Bengal cricket team and the East Zone. The 1987 Cricket
World Cup final was hosted in Eden Gardens. The Calcutta Cricket and Football Club is the second-oldest cricket club
in the world.
Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan (VYBK), is a multipurpose stadium in Kolkata, with a current capacity of 85,000. It
is the largest stadium in India by seating capacity. Before its renovation in 2011, it was the second-largest football
stadium in the world, having a seating capacity of 120,000. It has hosted many national and international sporting
events like the 1987 SAF Games, and the 2011 <color=#3366CC>FIFA</color> friendly football match between <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> and Venezuela, which
feature <color=#3366CC>Lionel Messi</color>. In 2008, the <color=#3366CC>German</color> goalkeeper, Oliver Kahn played his farewell match on this ground. The
stadium hosted the final match of the 2017 FIFA U-17 World Cup.
Notable sports persons from West Bengal include former Indian national cricket team captain Sourav Ganguly, Pankaj
Roy, Olympic tennis bronze medallist Leander Paes and chess grandmaster Dibyendu Barua.
Lewis Carroll
Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (27 January 1832 – 14 January 1898), better known by his pen name Lewis Carroll, was an
English author, poet, mathematician, photographer, and <color=#3366CC>Anglican</color> deacon. His most notable works are <color=#3366CC>Alice's</color>
<color=#3366CC>Adventures in Wonderland</color> (1865) and its sequel <color=#3366CC>Through the Looking-Glass</color> (1871), some of the most important
examples of Victorian literature. He was noted for his facility with <color=#3366CC>word play</color>, logic, and fantasy. His poems Jabberwocky
(1871) and The Hunting of the Snark (1876) are classified in the genre of literary nonsense. Some of Alice's
nonsensical wonderland logic reflects his published work on <color=#3366CC>mathematical logic</color>.
Carroll came from a family of high-church <color=#3366CC>Anglicans</color> and pursued his clerical training at Christ Church, Oxford, where
he lived for most of his life as a scholar, teacher and Anglican deacon (required for his academic fellowship at the time).
Alice Liddell – a daughter of Henry Liddell, the Dean of Christ Church – is widely identified as the original inspiration for
Alice in Wonderland, although Carroll always denied this.
An avid puzzler, Carroll created the word ladder puzzle, which he called "Doublets", which was published in Vanity Fair
magazine between 1879 and 1881. In 1982 a memorial stone to Carroll was unveiled at Poets' Corner in <color=#3366CC>Westminster</color>
<color=#3366CC>Abbey</color>. There are societies in many parts of the world dedicated to the enjoyment and promotion of his works.
Early life
Dodgson's family background was predominantly <color=#3366CC>northern English</color>, conservative, and high-church <color=#3366CC>Anglican</color>. Most of his
male ancestors were army officers or Anglican clergy. His great-grandfather, Charles Dodgson, had risen through the
ranks of the church to become the Bishop of Elphin in rural Ireland. His paternal grandfather, also named Charles, was
an army captain fatality of the Irish rebellion of 1803, when his two sons were hardly more than babies. The elder of
these sons, yet another Charles Dodgson, was Carroll's father. He went to Rugby School and then to Christ Church, a
constituent college of the <color=#3366CC>University of Oxford</color>. He reverted to the other family tradition and took <color=#3366CC>holy orders</color>. He was
mathematically gifted and won a double first degree. Instead of pursuing an academic career, he became a country
parson.
Dodgson was born on 27 January 1832 at All Saints' Vicarage in Daresbury, Cheshire, the oldest boy and the third
oldest of 11 children. When he was 11, his father was given the living of Croft-on-Tees, Yorkshire, and the whole family
moved to the spacious rectory. This remained their home for the next 25 years. Charles' father was an active and highly
conservative <color=#3366CC>cleric</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Church of England</color> who later became the Archdeacon of Richmond and involved himself,
sometimes influentially, in the intense religious disputes that were dividing the church. He was high-church, inclining
toward Anglo-Catholicism, an admirer of <color=#3366CC>John Henry Newman</color> and the Tractarian movement, and did his best to instil
such views in his children. However, Charles developed an ambivalent relationship with his father's values and with the
